Croxden
KROKS-den
n. (a Cistercian abbey in Staffordshire, founded 1176 by Bertram de Verdun; its chronicle claims the burial of King John's heart)
Old English personal name Croc with denu, a valley — Croc's valley.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Croxden was founded in 1176 by Bertram de Verdun, a daughter of Aunay in Normandy, and its church was built on the French plan with an apse and radiating chapels, unusual in England. Its chronicle, kept by the monk Thomas of Woodstock and others, is unusually detailed and records among much else the abbey's claim to hold the heart of King John, sent there after his death in 1216. Whether the claim is true matters less than the practice behind it, which was the division of a body among the houses that would pray for it, each taking a part and an endowment with it. Scripture has one thing to say about the heart, and it is not about burial. “Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life” (Pro 4:23) makes the heart the spring from which conduct flows, which is why its condition cannot be settled after death by anyone else. Our Lord traced the whole outward life to the same source: “For out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false witness, blasphemies” (Mat 15:19). A king who divided his heart among abbeys had not kept it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines heart as a muscular viscus, and figuratively the seat of the affections and passions, the inward or secret thoughts; and diligence as steady application in business of any kind.

expand to see more

HEART, n. A muscular viscus, which is the primary organ of the blood's motion. The inner part of any thing. The seat of the affections and passions.

DILIGENCE, n. Steady application in business of any kind; constant effort to accomplish what is undertaken.

ISSUE, n. The act of passing or flowing out; a moving out of any inclosed place. Event; consequence.

CHRONICLE, n. A historical account of facts or events disposed in the order of time.

INTERMENT, n. The act of depositing a dead body in the earth; burial; sepulture.

Key Scripture

Pro 4:23 — "Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life."

Mat 15:19 — "For out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false witness, blasphemies:"

Jer 17:9 — "The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?"

Eze 36:26 — "A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh."

Modern Corruption

A Staffordshire abbey that claimed a king's heart, and the one book that says what a heart is for.

expand to see more

The corruption is the dismembered burial — body in one church, heart in another, entrails in a third, each with land attached, so that the prayers of three communities might be bought at once. It treats intercession as quantity and the dead man as a portfolio. Behind it lies the deeper error, the belief that the heart's standing before God remains negotiable after death, when Scripture everywhere fixes it before: “The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?” (Jer 17:9).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that only God changes a heart, and he does it in this life by promise: “A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you” (Eze 36:26). That is the single remedy for a condition no endowment can touch, and it is offered to the living. The modern form of Croxden's error is the funeral that reassigns a man's standing by acclamation.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew leb (H3820), the heart; Hebrew mishmar (H4929), a guard or watch; Hebrew totsaah (H8444), an outgoing or issue; Greek kardia (G2588), the heart; Hebrew anash (H605), to be incurable.

expand to see more

Hebrew leb (H3820) — the heart, the inner man; “Keep thy heart with all diligence” (Pro 4:23).

Hebrew totsaah (H8444) — an outgoing, a source; “for out of it are the issues of life” (Pro 4:23).

Greek kardia (G2588) — the heart as the seat of thought and will; “For out of the heart proceed evil thoughts” (Mat 15:19).

Hebrew aqob (H6121) — deceitful, crooked; “The heart is deceitful above all things” (Jer 17:9).

Hebrew chadash (H2319) — new, fresh; “A new heart also will I give you” (Eze 36:26).

Usage

"“for out of it are the issues of life” (Pro 4:23) — why the heart is not a relic."

"“who can know it?” (Jer 17:9) — the question a tomb cannot answer."

"“and a new spirit will I put within you” (Eze 36:26) — the only transplant on offer."
